metadata.title: Counting The Wrong Words
metadata.subject: Market sentiment analysis — the measurement decision upstream of the model
metadata.primary_source: Loughran & McDonald, “When Is a Liability Not a Liability? Textual Analysis, Dictionaries, and 10-Ks”, The Journal of Finance LXVI(1), February 2011
metadata.title_note: Commissioned as “how to perform market sentiment analysis using AI for predicting stocks”, with permission to retitle. That bundles a method with a promised outcome. The method is routine; the measurement decision upstream of it is where the evidence is, and the prediction half is a separate claim the reel declines to make. B07 separates them.
metadata.scope_note: NOT INVESTMENT ADVICE. A measurement-methodology explainer. Names no tradable instrument, describes no strategy, reports no return or performance figure, and makes no claim that sentiment predicts prices.
metadata.note: ai-explainer spine, claude-hai channel, Weekly STEM. FRAMEWORK: three questions — WHAT COUNTS AS NEGATIVE AND WHO DECIDED / HOW MUCH IS A FEW COMMON WORDS / HAS ANYONE CHECKED IT PREDICTS ANYTHING. All figures read out of the Journal of Finance PDF directly with pdftotext; a search summary had mis-attributed 73.8% to distinct WORDS when the paper says word COUNTS, and that correction is the reason B03 labours the distinction. B08 grounds question 3 in the mycroft repo's own market-sentiment attestation, which states in writing that nobody has checked whether its score means anything.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. Speaks the author's name.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane. If you want to measure market sentiment with a model, the hardest decision is not which model. It is which words count as negative — and for years the most widely used answer to that question was measuring something else entirely.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the topic question, answered

shot.show: the Claude composer with the topic question and its three-line answer

props.command: claude "how do I do market sentiment analysis properly — what is the step people get wrong?"
props.segment: Uday Sonawane · Counting The Wrong Words
output: seven words were a quarter of it

beats.role_note: premise — the pipeline is easy, the measurement is the hard part
beats.narration_text: First, what the job actually is. A sentiment pipeline is four steps: get the text, count what you decided counts as negative, turn that into a score, and do something with it. Three of those are engineering. The second one is a measurement decision, it is made once, usually by inheriting somebody's word list, and everything downstream is built on top of it. If that list is wrong, a better model does not help you. It makes the wrong number more precisely.
beats.new_visual_element: the four steps, with the one that matters marked

shot.show: a four-step pipeline with step two singled out
shot.visual_intent: Four bordered boxes in a vertical chain, connected: get the text, count the negatives, make a score, act on it. The second is terracotta and wider, labelled 'a measurement decision, made once'. The other three carry a soft-ink chip reading 'engineering'.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions before trusting any sentiment number
beats.narration_text: Three questions before you trust a sentiment number. One: what counts as negative, and who decided — name the list. Two: how much of the score comes from a handful of common words — because a few frequent terms can carry most of it. Three: has anyone checked that the number predicts anything — which is a separate question from whether it measures tone, and it is usually the one nobody has answered.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: WHAT COUNTS AS NEGATIVE / HOW MUCH IS A FEW WORDS / HAS ANYONE CHECKED
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered cards land in a row, one per narration step. The first lands in terracotta — it is the decision the rest of the reel is about — and all three are the rubric the verdict is scored against.

beats.role_note: the headline result, stated with the precision the paper uses
beats.narration_text: Here is the measurement. A two thousand eleven paper in the Journal of Finance took the word list that textual analysis had been borrowing from psychology — the Harvard dictionary — and applied it to a hundred and twenty-one thousand annual filings. The finding: seventy-three point eight percent of the negative word counts came from words that are not typically negative in a financial context. Note what that percentage is of. Not of the word list. Of the counts — of the score itself.
beats.new_visual_element: the headline figure and what it is a percentage of

shot.show: 73.8% of negative word COUNTS, over 121,217 filings
shot.visual_intent: A large terracotta stat card reading 73.8%, captioned 'of the negative word COUNTS'. Beside it, two soft-ink cards: 121,217 filings, and 1994 to 2008. Beneath, one line in ink: 'not 73.8% of the list — of the score'. Citation strip names authors, journal and year.

beats.role_note: QUESTION 2 — the seven words, which is the detail that makes it concrete
beats.narration_text: And question two has an answer that is hard to forget. Seven words — tax, costs, loss, capital, cost, expense, expenses — account for more than a quarter of the entire negative count. The word costs on its own is four point six one percent of it. These are not sentiment. A company describing its tax position or its cost of capital is doing accounting. The dictionary was reading a balance sheet as a complaint.
beats.new_visual_element: the seven words and their share

shot.show: seven ordinary accounting words making up more than a quarter of the negativity
shot.visual_intent: Seven monospace word chips in two rows — tax, costs, loss, capital, cost, expense, expenses — in terracotta. Beneath, a bordered card reading 'more than one quarter of the total negative count', and a smaller chip: 'costs alone — 4.61%'. Cited.

beats.role_note: the other half of the failure — words that identify an industry, not a mood
beats.narration_text: There is a second failure mode in the same list, and it is worse than noise. Foreign, on that list, almost always means international operations. Vice usually introduces a vice-president. And words like mine, crude, tire and cancer do not identify a negative event at all — they identify an industry. So a mining company and an oil company score as gloomy by construction, every quarter, forever. That is not noise you can average away. It is a bias that lines up with the thing you are trying to measure.

shot.show: foreign, vice, mine, crude, tire, cancer — and what they actually indicate
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered rows. The first: foreign and vice, each with what they really mean — international operations, vice-presidents — in soft ink. The second, terracotta: mine, crude, tire, cancer, labelled 'these identify an industry, not an event'. Beneath, one line: a bias that does not average out. Cited.

beats.role_note: the fix, and the fact that it is smaller rather than bigger
beats.narration_text: The fix is the interesting part. The authors built a replacement negative list for finance — two thousand three hundred and thirty-seven words including inflections — and it is about half the size of the one it replaces. The improvement did not come from a bigger vocabulary or a bigger model. It came from someone sitting down with the domain and deciding, word by word, what actually means something bad here.
beats.new_visual_element: the replacement list and its size

shot.show: 2,337 words, about half the size of the list it replaces
shot.visual_intent: Two bars side by side, the Harvard list drawn roughly twice the length of the finance list beside it, the finance one in terracotta and labelled 2,337 words. Beneath, one line: 'smaller, and built by hand for the domain'. Cited.

beats.role_note: the limits — this fixes measurement, not prediction, and it is about filings
beats.narration_text: Now the limits, because this is where the original question gets its honest answer. This result is about annual filings. It does not automatically transfer to headlines, posts or earnings calls, which have different vocabularies. And more importantly: a better word list measures tone better. It does not establish that tone predicts prices. Those are two different claims, and only the first one is settled here. Measuring well is a precondition for predicting, not a substitute for testing whether you can.

shot.show: domain transfer, and measurement versus prediction
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered rows, each with a terracotta cross BESIDE it: 'this is about annual filings — other text has other vocabularies', and 'a better lexicon measures tone; it does not show tone predicts prices'. Beneath, one line in ink: measuring well is a precondition, not a substitute.

beats.role_note: QUESTION 3 scored against a live pipeline, then the two-sided verdict
beats.narration_text: Which brings question three home. The repository I make these weekly videos about contains a working market-sentiment pipeline, and its own attestation says this, in writing: nothing here asserts the number means anything — the weights, thresholds and keyword lists were inherited with no derivation, no backtest, and no author. That is this exact failure, live, in a real project, recorded honestly by the person who built it. So — be excited that the fix is tractable and costs domain attention rather than compute. Be sceptical of any sentiment number whose word list nobody can name.

beats.role_note: scaffolded task — defensive and checkable, aimed at the viewer's own pipeline
beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you have a sentiment score running anywhere, do one thing: sort its vocabulary by how much each term contributes to the total, and read the top twenty out loud. If most of them are ordinary nouns from the domain, you are measuring the domain, not the mood.
